opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Jesus says, "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me... Whoever finds his life will lose it."

Are you willing to let go of the life you've built for yourself so that I can give you the life I created you for?

If we spend our lives preserving our comfort, reputation, control, or possessions, we may succeed by the world's standards yet miss the very purpose for which we were created. But when we entrust our lives to Christ—even when it requires sacrifice—we begin to discover our true identity.

The cross is not simply suffering or misfortune. Everyone suffers. The cross is the cost of remaining faithful to Christ when that faithfulness demands surrender.

The question is not, "What is my cross?" but "How will I carry it?" Our crosses need not define us. Instead, they become the place where Christ reshapes us.
This is where the reading from the First Epistle of Peter comes alive. Peter writes: "He called you out of darkness into his marvelous light." Jesus says: "Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it."

They are describing the same journey. Peter speaks of a passage from darkness into light. Jesus speaks of a passage from the false self into the true self.
The darkness is the life centered on self—fear, control, pride, and the illusion that we can secure ourselves. The light is life in Christ, where our identity is no longer something we manufacture but something we receive.

In that sense, losing our life does not mean losing who we are. It means losing everything that keeps us from becoming who God intended us to be. The cross, then, is not the end of life. It is the path by which Christ leads us into it.

Yesterday I thought about the relationship between the brain and the soul. The brain naturally clings to what feels safe and familiar. It resists surrender because surrender feels like loss. But the soul recognizes Christ's voice and knows that what appears to be loss is actually the doorway to freedom. The Christian life is, in many ways, the lifelong work of allowing that deeper voice to lead the mind, until the light of Christ becomes stronger than the fears that once governed us.
